summary:
What did you develop?
Traces on the Moon and Mars: an interactive map of 27 spacecraft left on the Moon and Mars by 7 countries. Each point opens a card with a real NASA photo, the mission’s story and a voice from the spacecraft itself. Students collect stamps, answer quizzes, play games on real photos and earn a diploma.

How does it address the challenge?
It turns dry technical reports into short, living stories on a real map. Instead of reading data, students explore and play, and learn the history of old missions along the way.

Why is it important?
These spacecraft are humanity’s first traces on other worlds and part of our shared heritage. As people return to the Moon, we must remember and protect them. People only protect what they know.
details:
What it does and how it works
Traces on the Moon and Mars is an interactive web map of 27 spacecraft left on the Moon and Mars between 1959 and today. They come from seven countries: the USSR, USA, China, India, Japan, Israel and the UK.

Users switch between the Moon and Mars, filter spacecraft by status (still working, mission over, crashed or lost) and move a timeline slider from 1959 to 2026. Clicking a point opens an exhibit card with:

  • a real NASA or LRO photo;
  • the mission’s story;
  • what was left behind and why it matters;
  • a short first-person story told by the spacecraft, which can be read aloud.

Students collect stamps in an explorer passport, rise in rank, answer quiz questions and earn 18 awards. A Game Room offers three games on real NASA images:

  • Spot it in the photo;
  • Where did it land?;
  • Who was first?

The map also has a shared message wall (“What would you leave on the Moon?”), a class mode with a leaderboard, a section about spacecraft that are still lost, and a downloadable diploma.

Benefits
It turns dry technical reports into short, memorable stories. It makes learning active instead of passive and gives teachers a ready classroom activity. It is free, runs in any browser and is available in English and Russian.

Intended impact
We want people to remember humanity’s first traces on other worlds, not only new missions. As people return to the Moon, historic sites need protection, and people only protect what they know. We also hope to inspire young people to explore space and even search for the lost spacecraft themselves.

Tools and technologies

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no frameworks.
  • HTML Canvas, which draws the Moon and Mars surface maps and the personal diploma.
  • SVG icons and illustrations.
  • The Web Speech API for the spacecraft voices.
  • The browser’s local storage for each student’s progress.
  • The NASA Image and Video Library (images.nasa.gov) and LROC images from Arizona State University. Every photo is credited.
  • The claude.ai Artifacts platform for hosting, and its shared database for the message wall and class leaderboard.
  • Google Fonts.
  • Claude, an AI assistant, which helped us write code and edit texts.
  • Hardware: a regular laptop.

Creativity
Spacecraft “speak” about themselves, which turns machines into characters. The map works like a museum where every point is an exhibit. The games use real NASA photos, for example finding Neil Armstrong reflected in Buzz Aldrin’s visor. The “Find the lost ones” section turns an unsolved mystery into a challenge for students.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: we used open mission data and avoided invented facts. Where something is uncertain, we say so, and we correct popular myths, such as Opportunity’s “last words”.
  • Audience: simple language for school students.
  • Engagement: short visits had to turn into longer exploration.
  • Accessibility: it works on phones and computers and has alt text for images.
  • Privacy: messages ask for no surnames or contact details.
  • Fairness: spacecraft from all countries are included equally.
